blocks.text: Data Sources covered where data genuinely comes from, and the licensing and bias questions that come with any given origin. Even a well sourced, properly licensed dataset can still be genuinely unreliable once you actually look inside it, missing values, duplicate records, wrong units, inconsistent labels. Data Quality is the discipline of catching those problems before they quietly undermine everything built on top of the data.

This topic covers the genuine dimensions that make up data quality, the different reasons values end up missing in the first place, why duplicate records are a genuinely easy problem to miss, and the profiling habits that catch quality problems early, before a model has a chance to learn them as if they were real signal.
1. The Six Genuine Dimensions of Data Quality

blocks.alt: The Six Genuine Dimensions of Data Quality
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442992979-358767642.png

Completeness asks whether the values that should genuinely be present actually are, an age column with a third of its entries blank has a genuine completeness problem. Accuracy asks whether the values that are present are genuinely correct, an age of 250 recorded for a customer is present but obviously not accurate.

Consistency asks whether the same real world thing is represented the same way everywhere, a country field that lists both USA and United States for the same country is genuinely inconsistent. Timeliness asks whether the data is still genuinely current, a customer address from five years ago may no longer reflect reality. Uniqueness asks whether the same real observation appears only once, not duplicated. Validity asks whether a value genuinely fits its expected range or format, a negative age or an invalid email address both fail this test.

blocks.text: 2. Why Values Genuinely End Up Missing

blocks.alt: Why Values Genuinely End Up Missing
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442992979-845896988.png

Not all missing values happen for the same genuine reason, and the reason matters for how safely they can be handled later. Some values are genuinely missing at random, a sensor briefly disconnected with no pattern behind which readings were lost. Others are missing in a way genuinely related to another column, income might be more often missing for younger respondents specifically, a real pattern rather than pure randomness.

The hardest genuine case is when a value is missing precisely because of what its own true value would have been, income being disproportionately missing for genuinely very high earners who chose not to disclose it. This last case is the most dangerous, because filling it in with an average would genuinely bias the result in a specific, misleading direction.

blocks.title: Why this distinction matters
blocks.content: Filling every missing value the same way, say, with the column average, genuinely ignores which of these three cases you are actually in. The wrong choice can quietly introduce a real bias rather than remove one.

blocks.text: 3. Duplicate Records: A Genuinely Easy Problem to Miss

blocks.alt: Duplicate Records: A Genuinely Easy Problem to Miss
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442992980-689462447.png

A duplicate record, the same real observation appearing more than once, is a genuinely common and genuinely easy to overlook quality problem, especially after combining multiple sources, exactly the situation covered in the previous topic. Duplicates do not just waste space, they genuinely distort any statistic computed over the dataset, an average, a count, a proportion, all get pulled toward whatever got duplicated.

Duplicates are not always exact, character for character copies either, the same customer might appear once as "Jane Smith" and once as "J. Smith", genuinely the same person recorded slightly differently, a harder, near duplicate case that requires more care to catch than a simple identical row check.
4. A Worked Example
A small, genuinely realistic customer dataset shows several quality problems at once, exactly the kind a quick profiling pass should catch before the data goes anywhere near a model.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "customer_id": [1, 2, 3, 3, 5],
    "age": [29, 250, None, 31, -4],
    "country": ["USA", "United States", "USA", "USA", "usa"],
})

print("Missing values per column:")
print(df.isnull().sum())

print("Duplicate rows:")
print(df.duplicated(subset="customer_id").sum())

print("Values outside a genuinely plausible age range:")
print(df[(df["age"] < 0) | (df["age"] > 120)])

blocks.text: This one small table genuinely has a missing age, an implausible age of 250, a negative age, a duplicated customer_id, and three genuinely inconsistent spellings of the same country. Every single one of these is exactly the kind of problem the profiling habits in this topic are meant to catch early.
5. Garbage In, Garbage Out
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442992980-971320339.png

This is genuinely one of the oldest, truest sayings in computing, and it applies to machine learning with real force. A model trained on data with undetected quality problems does not somehow correct those problems on its own, it genuinely learns them as if they were real signal, an implausible age of 250 gets treated by the model exactly like a genuinely valid data point, quietly distorting whatever the model eventually learns.

This is precisely why data quality deserves real, deliberate attention before feature engineering or modeling ever begins, catching a quality problem after a model has already been trained on it is far more costly than catching it here, at the source, before it has a chance to spread through every downstream step.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: A model cannot genuinely tell the difference between real signal and an undetected data quality problem. It will learn both equally well, which is exactly why quality has to be checked by a person, or a deliberate process, before training ever starts.

blocks.text: 6. Profiling: Catching Problems Before They Spread

blocks.alt: Profiling: Catching Problems Before They Spread
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442993381-58523807.png

Profiling a new dataset means running a genuinely quick, standard set of checks before doing anything else with it, checking missing value counts per column, checking summary statistics for genuinely odd values like a maximum age of 250, and checking that each column data type genuinely matches what it should hold, a date column that is secretly stored as text is a genuinely common, easy to miss profiling catch.

This habit does not need to be elaborate to be genuinely effective, even the three simple checks in the worked example above catch a real majority of common quality problems, and running them takes only a few minutes against the real cost of discovering the same problems much later, buried inside a trained model behavior.

blocks.text: 7. Consistency Across Formats and Units
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442993382-723737754.png

A genuinely common, specific consistency problem arises when the same field is recorded differently across sources or even within one source, one system logging price in dollars, another in cents, one date column formatted day first, another month first. Left unreconciled, this kind of mismatch does not look like an obvious error, the values are all genuinely plausible numbers, just measured on different scales.

This is exactly the kind of problem that survives a casual glance at the data and only shows up once someone actually computes a statistic that mixes the two scales together, an average price that is wildly wrong because half the rows were secretly in cents. Reconciling every field to one consistent unit and format is a genuinely necessary step before any real analysis begins.
8. Data Quality Versus What Comes Next

blocks.alt: Data Quality Versus What Comes Next
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442993382-834073470.png

Everything covered here, completeness, accuracy, consistency, duplicates, deals with problems that are genuinely visible once you look for them, a missing value count, a duplicate row, an implausible age, all show up under direct inspection. The next topic covers a genuinely sneakier failure mode, one that can pass every check in this topic and still quietly ruin a model.

Data Leakage happens when information that should never genuinely be available at prediction time accidentally slips into training, a problem that a dataset can have while looking completely clean by every measure covered in this topic, which is exactly why it deserves its own dedicated topic next.

items: Data quality genuinely has six dimensions: completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness, and validity.
Missing values can be genuinely random, related to another column, or related to their own true value, each needing different handling.
Duplicate records genuinely distort statistics and are easy to miss, especially after combining sources.
A model trained on undetected quality problems genuinely learns those problems as if they were real signal.
Profiling a new dataset, checking missing counts, summary statistics, and data types, catches most common problems early.
The next topic, Data Leakage, covers a genuinely sneakier failure that can hide behind an otherwise clean dataset.
